title: The Handful of Auctions That Ended Souq.com's eBay Years
dek: After a year of watching its own numbers, Souq.com dropped the auctions it was known for at the start of 2011 and began turning itself into a retailer.

story.event: Ending auctions for fixed-price selling and then stocking goods itself
story.summary: Souq.com, founded in Dubai in 2005 and long called the eBay of the Middle East, ended auctions at the start of 2011 after its chief executive Ronaldo Mouchawar said about a year of analysis showed few auction sales. Later in 2011 it began buying, stocking and shipping popular products itself. It grew into the region's largest online retailer and was bought by Amazon in 2017.
paragraphs: In November 2010 only a handful of auctions closed on Souq.com, the Dubai site long called the eBay of the Middle East. Its chief executive, Ronaldo Mouchawar, said that was when he made up his mind. "I had to be personally convinced," he told The National a few weeks later. From the start of 2011, sellers could no longer offer goods at auction; everything would carry a fixed price.

Souq had begun in 2005 with five employees, incubated within Maktoob, the Arab web portal. Mouchawar later called it "a very simple listings site till about 2009". That year Yahoo bought Maktoob and Souq went its own way. By late 2010 he could see about 120,000 products listed against some 5,000 auctions, and few auction sales in recent months. Most buyers in the region, the company said, wanted to buy at once, and fixed prices allowed better search, quicker checkout, reviews and price comparison. It had taken, he said, about twelve months of analysis.

Five years on he remembered it more starkly. He said he had told his team: "We have to shut down auction in the next three months. If we don't, we'll be obsolete in two years." The money they had went into the new product. "Either we'd make it or we'd all go home." Sellers rang to complain, he recalled. Accounts differ on what was given up: at the time The National reported few auctions selling, while Entrepreneur Middle East later described the auctions and classifieds Souq closed as significant sources of traffic and revenue.

By October 2011 Souq had gone further, starting to buy and stock its most popular products, take payment and ship goods itself, and investing in warehouses. By 2015 it listed more than a million products from over 70,000 vendors and employed more than 2,000 people, and by early 2016 it had raised $425 million from investors including Tiger Global and Naspers. In March 2017 Amazon agreed to buy it. The price was not disclosed; Arab News later put it at $580 million, and the Financial Times reported about $650 million.

quote.text: If by leaving a small pleasure one sees a great pleasure, let a wise man leave the small pleasure, and look to the great.
quote.source_title: Dhammapada, a Collection of Verses, tr. F. Max Müller, Project Gutenberg eBook #2017
quote.connection: The verse sets a condition before its advice: first one has to see the greater thing. Mouchawar spent a year looking before he let the auctions go, and the sellers who rang to complain were still giving up something they valued.

reflection: Mouchawar's decision looks obvious from 2017. In November 2010 it meant closing the feature the site was known for, while sellers rang to say they were unhappy. What he had was a year of watching his own numbers, and a month when the numbers and his own conviction finally agreed.

Most of us keep something going long after we suspect it has stopped serving us: a weekly meeting, a side project, a way of doing a task that made sense two years ago. The verse asks for something modest first, which is to see what the larger thing would be. You do not have to stop anything today. You can start keeping count.
invitation: Pick one routine or piece of work you keep going out of habit. For the next two weeks, note each time it actually helps someone, and look at the tally before deciding anything.

cross_checks.claim: Souq.com started in 2005 as an eBay-style auction and listings site linked to Maktoob.
From the start of 2011 Souq ended auctions and sold only at fixed prices.
Yahoo bought Maktoob in 2009 and Souq went on independently.
Mouchawar describes the decision as stopping things that were working in order to become a business-to-customer retailer.
Amazon agreed to buy Souq in March 2017; the price was undisclosed, with reports of $580 million and about $650 million.

research_notes: Retry of an entry dropped earlier for want of Mouchawar's own account. It is now sourced from contemporary reporting (The National and The Next Web, January 2011) that quotes him, and from his later interviews (The National 2015, Entrepreneur Middle East 2017, Arab News 2022). The date of the decision: The National's 2 January 2011 report quotes him deciding 'after only a handful of auctions closed', with the paper's bracket '[in November]', so November 2010; The Next Web says auctions ended from the beginning of 2011. His 2015 recollection of telling the team to shut auctions within three months fits that window. What auctions were worth is disputed: in January 2011 The National reported few auction sales and about 5,000 auctions against 120,000 listings; Entrepreneur Middle East (2017) described the closed auction and classifieds services as 'fairly significant generators of both traffic and revenue'; Arabian Business, in a page that returns 403 and could not be read, is reported to quote him saying Souq lost 80 per cent of its revenue in one night. The story gives the first two with attribution and leaves out the unread 80 per cent figure. Amazon price: undisclosed; Arab News (2022) and Africanews (2019) give $580 million, Entrepreneur Middle East cites the Financial Times at about $650 million, and other outlets (not cited) gave figures up to about $700 million; the story gives the two cited figures. Founding year is 2005 in every source cited (one earlier note found 2007 in Daily News Egypt, not cited). Arab News says Souq was founded with investment from Maktoob co-founder Samih Toukan; the story credits Mouchawar as founder, as all the cited sources do, and does not name co-founders. The Dhammapada verse is applied by analogy.
